title: Routing and Ownership Playbook for Control Plane Boundaries
content:
Purpose:
This is a working playbook sketch to clarify service boundaries and ownership for the control plane pieces that touch routing policies, orchestration, and runtime adapters. Goal is pragmatic: reduce cross-team ambiguity when adding features (routing rules, failover, model variants) and make ownership explicit for incidents and rollout coordination across regions.

Audience and context:
- Primary audience: platform-engineering, serving-runtime, infra, and SRE on-call.
- Secondary: product owners for Dedicated/Private and Solutions Eng when we need custom routing.
- This doc is intentionally informal; use it as the starting point for a formal ownership map we capture in Confluence.

High-level decomposition (opinions, not gospel):
1) Edge/API Gateway (layer-7 ingress)
   - Responsibility: public client-facing ingress, authentication, rate-limiting, global routing decisions based on client attributes (region, plan), basic feature flags.
   - Owns: TLS termination, JWT/OAuth verification, primary geo DNS handoff, rate-limits counters and quota enforcement hooks.
   - Examples of decisions it should make: route to hosted vs dedicated endpoints, prefer low-latency region for free-tier users, strip/annotate headers for downstream policies.
   - Not owning: token-level cost accounting, deep model routing heuristics, circuit-breaker to runtime internals.

2) Control Plane Orchestration (control-plane service)
   - Responsibility: decisioning brain for model selection, rollout policies (canary, A/B), autoscaler controls, and routing policy evaluation that requires system state (capacity, model health, SLOs).
   - Owns: policy store, rollout config API, reconciliation loops with region clusters, orchestration of fallback chains across model variants.
   - Interfaces upstream: API Gateway calls orchestration to evaluate policy when decisions need state beyond request metadata.
   - Interfaces downstream: instructs runtime adapters, pushes configuration to edge caches, and emits telemetry for Console.

3) Runtime Adapters (per-execution-plane connectors)
   - Responsibility: translate orchestration decisions into concrete runtime actions (select model binary, quantization variant, GPU queue, or a fallback shard).
   - Owns: adapter code per runtime flavor (hosted-runtime, dedicated-agent, private-connector), capability negotiation, health checks, and perf hinting for batching.
   - Important: adapters run near the runtime (region or VPC) — they must be robust to network partitions and expose the minimal control surface for orchestration to query.

4) Regional Control Agents (lightweight controllers near runtime)
   - Responsibility: local enforcement of routing decisions, local capacity accounting, fast failover when cross-region calls are unavailable.
   - Owns: local cache of hot policies, short-circuit failover rules, KV-cache invalidation requests from orchestration.

Routing policy placement guidance (when to evaluate where):
- Evaluate at edge (API Gateway) when: decision is stateless, fast, and only requires request metadata (plan, path, client region). Keep evaluation < 5ms target.
- Evaluate in orchestration when: decision requires cluster capacity, model health, rollout state, or cost tradeoffs. Expect < 50ms for non-pathological cases, but plan for async/cached answers for high QPS paths.
- Evaluate in regional agents when: need for millisecond-level failover, or to avoid cross-region calls during partitions.

Common routing patterns and owner responsibilities:
- Prefer-nearest-region: edge provides candidate region list, orchestration returns preferred region based on SLOs, regional agent enforces and reports. (Orchestration owns policy; infra owns DNS/anycast config; adapters implement selection.)
- Cost-based routing: orchestration evaluates expected unit cost and signals to adapters. (Orchestration owns policy + economics dataset; finance provides pricing feed.)
- Model-variant rollouts: orchestration owns rollout config; adapters must support shadow/traffic-split modes; gateway must tag traffic for tracing.

Decision surface: who can change what without cross-team coordination?
- Safe changes (owner only): adapter health check thresholds, local cache TTLs, minor telemetry labels.
- Requires notification: rollout config changes > 5% traffic shift, adding a new region as primary, global rate-limit policy updates.
- Requires cross-team review: schema changes to policy store, introducing new routing predicates that call external systems (billing, third-party signals).

Telemetry and SLOs (minimum requirements):
- Edge: request latencies, auth failures, rate-limit rejections, region selection distribution. Owner: infra/edge team.
- Orchestration: policy-eval latency histogram, decision divergence counts (edge vs orchestration), config reconcile errors. Owner: platform-orchestration team.
- Runtime adapters: model-selection latency, adapter-sidefallbacks, queue length, per-model token throughput. Owner: runtime-adapters team.
- Region agents: cache hit rate for policies, local failover activations. Owner: platform-engineering (regional ops subteam).

Ownership map (short matrix) - rough:
- API Gateway: infra/edge (owner: Miguel Alvarez)
- Orchestration service (policy engine): platform-orchestration (owner: Priya Ramanathan)
- Runtime adapters: serving-runtime team (owner: Sara Liu)
- Regional control agents: platform-engineering / regional-ops (owner: Ethan Park)
- Console / Telemetry: observability team (owner: Casey Nguyen)

Operational play examples (quick runbook snippets):
1) Traffic is suddenly routed to wrong model variant in eu-west-1:
   - Step 1: on-call edge checks recent policy-eval logs and tags from gateway (owner: infra).
   - Step 2: orchestration runbook: validate rollout config -> if drifted, roll back to previous commit and notify runtime adapters.
   - Step 3: adapters: force-local model pin for critical tenants until root cause identified.
   - Postmortem: decide whether the rollout API needs stricter guards (owner: platform-orchestration).

2) Inter-region partition causing orchestration timeouts:
   - Allow regional agents to continue enforcement using cached policies. Fallback strategy: prefer local region with degraded capacity threshold 20%.
   - Notify Console and set incident severity if more than 5% of requests hit degraded enforcement.

Open questions / unresolved tradeoffs:
- How much logic should live in the edge vs orchestration for per-tenant ML-optimized routing? (Performance vs central visibility).
- Do we version the policy DSL? If so, what is a safe migration path for agents that lag?
- How to make cost-based routing transparent to product teams (explainability for billing calls)?
- For Private deployments, adapater contract surface must be minimal — what subset of the policy language is reasonable to expose?

Next actions / owner TODOs:
- Priya: draft a short Confluence page with the matrix above and attach this playbook (due 2026-02-20).
- Miguel: propose minimal edge predicate set we allow at edge (due 2026-02-28).
- Sara: list adapter capability matrix and backward compatibility guarantees (WIP PR referenced above).
- Ethan: prototype local-agent cache TTL tuning and failure-mode behavior against simulated partitions.

Notes to self / meeting pointers:
- Bring this to platform-arch working group on Fri 2026-02-12; agenda: ownership matrix, decision surface, rollout guardrails.
- Share with SRE on-call rota for feedback about runbook steps.

Appendix: quick glossary (informal)
- Policy store: single source of truth for routing/rollout policies.
- Adapter: code that maps policy decisions to runtime parameters.
- Regional agent: lightweight controller that caches policy and enforces short-circuit rules.

Rough references we used while drafting (tickets / PRs):
- PLAT-4123: initial policy-store schema change
- PR #789: adapter capability negotiation prototype
- Slack thread: #platform-arch "routing fallback discussion"

End (working draft).

Feedback welcome — add inline comments in the Confluence draft or ping me in Slack.
